stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Astronomers at a high-altitude observatory spent three clear nights tracking a faint comet as it swung toward the Sun, measuring how quickly its tail lengthened. On the fourth night, a bank of clouds settled over the mountain ______ team used the lost observing time to recalibrate the telescope's camera and check the previous nights' measurements for errors.
explanation: "On the fourth night, a bank of clouds settled over the mountain" can stand alone as a sentence, and so can "the team used the lost observing time to recalibrate..." When two complete sentences meet, a semicolon is one of the correct ways to join them, so you should pick the semicolon.

A.why: You went with the comma because the break sounds like a short pause. But both sides are complete sentences, and a comma alone can't join two sentences. This is a comma splice.

C.why: You left out the punctuation, which runs two complete sentences together into a run-on. A boundary is needed between "mountain" and "the team."

D.why: You saw that "and" can join two sentences, but a FANBOYS word between two complete sentences needs a comma in front of it. Without the comma, this is still a run-on.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In traditional Japanese woodblock printing, the artist's design was transferred to several blocks of cherry wood, and a separate block was carved for every color. A single landscape print might require a dozen of these ______ one had to line up exactly with the others, or the colors would overlap and blur the image's fine edges.
explanation: "A single landscape print might require a dozen of these blocks" is a complete sentence. "Each one had to line up exactly with the others..." is also a complete sentence. A comma plus the FANBOYS word "and" is a correct way to join two sentences, so this is the answer.

A.why: You treated "each one had to line up..." as a description of the blocks. But it has its own subject ("each one") and verb ("had"), so it's a full sentence. Joining it to another sentence with only a comma makes a comma splice.

B.why: With no punctuation, the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on. You need a boundary between "blocks" and "each."

D.why: You knew a comma and "and" belonged together, but you put the comma on the wrong side. It has to come before the conjunction. Here it lands after "and," so it doesn't mark the boundary between the two sentences.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To prepare for a regional measles vaccination drive, a district health office trained nearly two hundred community health workers. Those workers visited more than four thousand rural households over the course of the six-week ______ door to door, they logged each child's immunization history on a shared tablet so that clinics could identify any doses that had been missed.
explanation: "Those workers visited more than four thousand rural households over the course of the six-week campaign" is a complete sentence. What follows also has its own subject and verb ("they logged"), so it is a second complete sentence that happens to open with "Working door to door." A period correctly separates the two.

A.why: The participle "working" made the second half look like a modifier attached to the first sentence. Read on, though, and "they logged" shows it's a complete sentence. That makes this comma a comma splice.

B.why: With no punctuation, the first sentence runs straight into the second, which creates a run-on. You need a full stop before "Working."

C.why: You tried to join the two sentences with "and" but left out the comma that has to come before it, so the result is still a run-on. Inserting "and" also makes "working door to door" read awkwardly as if it continued the first clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: After the body fights off an infection, most of the immune cells that attacked the invader die within a few weeks. A small population of memory B cells, however, can survive in the bone marrow for decades after the ______ long lifespan allows the immune system to produce antibodies within days, rather than weeks, if the same pathogen ever returns.
explanation: "A small population of memory B cells, however, can survive in the bone marrow for decades after the infection" is a complete sentence. "This long lifespan allows the immune system to produce antibodies..." is a complete sentence too. A semicolon is a correct way to join two complete sentences.

B.why: The two ideas are closely related, so a comma felt like enough. A comma alone still can't join two complete sentences, however closely linked they are. This is a comma splice.

C.why: Leaving out the punctuation fuses two complete sentences into a run-on. You need a boundary before "this."

D.why: "And" can join two sentences only if a comma comes before it. Without that comma, this choice is still a run-on.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sea otters along the Pacific coast often rest in groups, called rafts, that float just beyond the breaking waves. Before dozing off, an otter will roll over several times to wrap itself in strands of giant kelp that are anchored to the seafloor. Researchers believe the animals do this to stay in place while they ______ keeps them from drifting out of their feeding grounds on the tide.
explanation: "Researchers believe the animals do this to stay in place while they sleep" is a complete sentence. "The kelp keeps them from drifting out of their feeding grounds on the tide" is another one. A period correctly separates them.

A.why: A comma seemed like a natural pause after "sleep," but there is a complete sentence on each side. A bare comma between them is a comma splice.

B.why: With no punctuation, the reader can't tell where the first sentence ends, and the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on.

D.why: You treated "then" as a joining word. It isn't a FANBOYS conjunction, though, so a comma plus "then" still can't join two complete sentences. This is still a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When a county health department reviewed its records from a season of free flu vaccination clinics, analysts found a clear pattern in who had shown up. Clinics open only on weekday mornings drew few working adults ______ clinics that stayed open into the evening vaccinated nearly twice as many people in that age group. The department has since moved most of its clinic hours to late afternoons and weekends.
explanation: Cover the blank and test each side. "Clinics open only on weekday mornings drew few working adults" is a complete sentence, and so is "clinics that stayed open into the evening vaccinated nearly twice as many people in that age group." Two complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon, so "adults; clinics" is correct.

A.why: You put no punctuation between two complete sentences, which makes a run-on. The reader can't tell where the first thought ends.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. The comma sounds like a natural pause, but a comma alone can't join two complete sentences.

D.why: "However" signals the right contrast, but it's an adverb, not a FANBOYS conjunction. With only commas around it, this is still a comma splice. It would need a semicolon before "however."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorist Ines Vardakis spent three summers recording the bedtime stories that grandparents tell in the mountain villages of western Crete. Nearly every storyteller she interviewed described the same trickster, a fox who outwits a greedy miller ______ details of the tale shifted from one village to the next. In some versions the fox steals flour, and in others it tricks the miller into giving away his mill.
explanation: The words before the blank form a complete sentence ("Nearly every storyteller . . . described the same trickster"). The words after it do too ("the details of the tale shifted from one village to the next"). A comma followed by a FANBOYS word is a legal join, and "but" fits the contrast between a shared character and changing details. That makes "miller, but the" correct.

A.why: You chose a comma splice. Because the comma sits right after the phrase about the fox, it can feel like part of that description, but what follows is a separate complete sentence.

B.why: With no punctuation, the two complete sentences run together, and "miller the details" reads as one garbled phrase. That's a run-on.

D.why: You picked the right conjunction but put the comma on the wrong side. The comma has to come before "but" to join the two sentences. A comma after "but" breaks the clause at a point where no punctuation belongs.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: While excavating a Bronze Age settlement on the banks of the Vistula River in northern Poland, archaeologists uncovered more than two hundred clay spindle whorls ______ small weights like these were once fitted onto wooden spindles to help twist raw wool and flax into thread. The sheer number found in ordinary houses suggests that spinning was a daily chore in nearly every household.
explanation: Before the blank there is a complete sentence: the long opening "While excavating . . ." phrase is attached to the main clause "archaeologists uncovered more than two hundred clay spindle whorls." After the blank there is another complete sentence with its own subject ("small weights like these") and verb ("were fitted"). A period correctly separates them.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. "Small weights like these" can look like a description of the whorls, but it is the subject of a new sentence with its own verb, "were fitted." A comma alone can't join the two sentences.

C.why: With no punctuation at all, the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on. The long first sentence doesn't make a break unnecessary.

D.why: "And" is a FANBOYS word, but when it joins two complete sentences it needs a comma before it. Without one, these two long independent clauses run together.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorist Ines Varga spent three summers recording bedtime stories in villages along the Danube. She found that one tale about a clever goose survives in at least eleven local ______ outwits a different enemy in each, from a hungry fox to a greedy tax collector.
explanation: Cover the blank and test each side. "She found that one tale about a clever goose survives in at least eleven local versions" can stand alone as a sentence. So can "the goose outwits a different enemy in each." When there is a complete sentence on each side, a semicolon is one of the correct ways to join them. The singular subject "goose" also matches the singular verb "outwits."

A.why: This is a comma splice. Both sides are complete sentences, and a comma on its own can't join them. You probably picked it because the comma sounds like a natural pause.

B.why: This runs two complete sentences together with no punctuation, which makes a fused sentence. You lost track of where the first sentence ends and the second one begins.

D.why: The semicolon is correct here, but "geese" is plural and the verb "outwits" is singular, so they don't agree. The passage is also about one goose. You looked at the punctuation and skipped the word after it.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In 2019, economist Darnell Okafor surveyed warehouse workers in four states about their schedules. Most respondents were working the same number of hours each week as they had a year ______ shifts were now posted, on average, only three days in advance, which made childcare and second jobs hard to arrange.
explanation: "Most respondents were working the same number of hours each week as they had a year earlier" is a complete sentence. So is "Their shifts were now posted, on average, only three days in advance." When both sides can stand alone, a period is a correct way to separate them.

A.why: This is a comma splice: a bare comma between two complete sentences. The comma matches where you would pause when reading aloud, but pausing isn't the test. Check whether each side can stand alone.

C.why: With no punctuation, the two sentences fuse into a run-on. You may have read "earlier their shifts" as one phrase and missed that a new subject starts at "their."

D.why: A comma plus "so" is a legal way to join two sentences, but "so" says the second fact is caused by the first. Working the same hours doesn't cause shifts to be posted late. The join is grammatical, but the logic doesn't fit.
